name: SOC 2
one_line_summary: AICPA framework for reporting on controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy.
extended_summary: SOC 2 is the AICPA's reporting framework for evaluating controls at service organizations against the Trust Services Criteria (TSC), which span Security (the only mandatory category), Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy. Reports come in two types: Type 1 attests to control design at a point in time, while Type 2 attests to operating effectiveness across a defined period (typically 6-12 months). SOC 2 emerged in 2011 alongside SOC 1 and SOC 3 as part of the AICPA's restructuring of its service-organization reporting framework, replacing the older SAS 70. Reports are conducted under SSAE 18 attestation standards by licensed CPAs and have become a near-universal contractual requirement for B2B SaaS, cloud infrastructure, managed services, and other technology service providers.
originators: American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA)
year_or_decade: 2011 (SOC framework introduced); Trust Services Criteria 2017 (current revision with 2022 points of focus update)
core_components: Trust Services Criteria (Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy); Type 1 (point-in-time design) vs Type 2 (operating effectiveness over period); Common Criteria (mandatory) plus category-specific criteria; Complementary user entity controls (CUECs); Subservice organization controls (carve-out vs inclusive); SSAE 18 attestation framework
primary_use_case: Customer-facing assurance for service organizations (especially SaaS and cloud providers) demonstrating control effectiveness; common contractual requirement in vendor risk management.
common_criticisms: Scope is auditor- and management-defined, allowing meaningful exclusions; report quality and rigor vary widely across audit firms; cost can be prohibitive for early-stage providers; point-in-time and period-based assurance does not cover real-time control effectiveness; criteria language allows substantial interpretation latitude; can become a marketing artifact more than a security signal.
primary_sources: AICPA (2017, updated 2022). Trust Services Criteria for Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy; AICPA. SSAE 18: Attestation Standards: Clarification and Recodification (effective 2017)
siblings: ISO/IEC 27001; HITRUST CSF; SSAE 18; NIST Cybersecurity Framework

name: SSAE 18
one_line_summary: Statement on Standards for Attestation Engagements 18 — current AICPA standard governing service organization audits.
extended_summary: SSAE 18 is the AICPA Auditing Standards Board's 2016 statement that consolidated and clarified the attestation standards previously contained in SSAE 10-17 and SSAE 16, recodifying them into the AT-C section structure (AT-C 105 common concepts, AT-C 205 examination engagements, AT-C 305 agreed-upon procedures, AT-C 320 reporting on controls at a service organization). It is the standard under which SOC 1, SOC 2, and SOC 3 examinations are conducted, and it materially strengthened requirements around service auditor responsibilities for subservice organizations (complementary subservice organization controls — CSOCs), monitoring of subservice organizations by service organizations, and consideration of the risks of material misstatement. Subsequent statements (SSAE 19 through SSAE 22) have refined specific aspects without replacing the SSAE 18 framework as the primary attestation standard for SOC reporting.
originators: American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) Auditing Standards Board
core_components: AT-C 105 (concepts common to all attestation engagements); AT-C 205 (examination engagements); AT-C 305 (agreed-upon procedures engagements); AT-C 320 (reporting on examinations of controls at service organizations); Complementary subservice organization controls (CSOCs); Risk-of-material-misstatement assessment; Subservice organization monitoring requirements; Carve-out and inclusive method for subservice presentation
primary_use_case: Professional standard governing CPA-performed attestation engagements, most prominently SOC 1, SOC 2, and SOC 3 reports on service organization controls.
common_criticisms: Codification complexity creates interpretation variability across firms; CSOC requirements imposed substantial monitoring burden on service organizations using subservice providers; less prescriptive than ISO 27001 on specific control objectives; AICPA scope limits international portability of SOC reports; standards layered through multiple subsequent SSAEs creates navigability friction.
primary_sources: AICPA (2016). Statement on Standards for Attestation Engagements No. 18: Attestation Standards: Clarification and Recodification

name: TCFD
aliases: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
one_line_summary: Voluntary framework for climate-related financial risk disclosures across governance, strategy, risk, and metrics.
extended_summary: The TCFD was established by the Financial Stability Board in 2015 under the chairmanship of Michael Bloomberg to develop voluntary, consistent climate-related financial risk disclosures for companies, banks, insurers, and asset owners. Its 2017 final recommendations organized disclosures around four thematic pillars — Governance, Strategy, Risk Management, and Metrics & Targets — with eleven recommended disclosures and supplemental guidance for the financial sector and four non-financial sectors. The framework distinguishes between physical risks (acute and chronic climate impacts) and transition risks (policy, technology, market, and reputational shifts associated with decarbonization), and recommends scenario analysis including a 2°C-or-lower scenario. The TCFD was disbanded in 2023 with monitoring of disclosures transferred to the IFRS Foundation, whose ISSB has since published IFRS S1 and S2 incorporating and extending the TCFD recommendations as a mandatory baseline.
originators: Financial Stability Board (FSB); Task Force chaired by Michael Bloomberg
core_components: Four pillars: Governance; Strategy; Risk Management; Metrics & Targets; Eleven recommended disclosures; Distinction between physical and transition risk; Scenario analysis (including 2°C-or-lower); Sector-specific supplemental guidance for financial and four non-financial sectors
primary_use_case: Voluntary climate-related financial disclosures incorporated into supervisory expectations (Bank of England PRA, NGFS, ECB), national mandatory regimes (UK 2022 mandatory TCFD-aligned disclosure), and the ISSB's IFRS S1/S2 successor standards.
common_criticisms: Voluntary nature and qualitative framing produced uneven adoption and disclosure quality; scenario analysis methodology under-specified, creating comparability problems; metric specifications thin in early versions; superseded by IFRS S2 from ISSB which formalizes much of the framework with greater specificity; integration with Scope 3 emissions disclosure remained contested.
primary_sources: TCFD (2017). Recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures; TCFD (2021). Implementing the Recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (revised guidance)

name: SASB
one_line_summary: Industry-specific sustainability disclosure standards, now under the IFRS Foundation's ISSB.
extended_summary: SASB Standards are industry-specific sustainability disclosure standards developed for use by US-listed companies and their investors, covering 77 industries organized into 11 sectors via the Sustainable Industry Classification System (SICS). SASB was founded in 2011 by Jean Rogers as a US analogue to the FASB for sustainability information, focused explicitly on financial materiality to the reasonable investor — distinguishing it from the broader stakeholder orientation of GRI. After codification of its standards in 2018, SASB merged with the International Integrated Reporting Council in 2021 to form the Value Reporting Foundation, which was then consolidated into the IFRS Foundation in 2022 to form the basis of the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB). SASB Standards are now maintained as part of the ISSB's framework and are referenced in IFRS S1 (general sustainability) for industry-specific disclosure topics.
originators: Jean Rogers (founder); SASB Foundation; subsequently Value Reporting Foundation (2021); IFRS Foundation/ISSB (2022 onward)
year_or_decade: 2011 (founded); 2018 (codified standards); 2021 (merger into VRF); 2022 (consolidation into IFRS Foundation)
core_components: 77 industry standards across 11 sectors; Sustainable Industry Classification System (SICS); Industry-specific disclosure topics and accounting metrics; Five sustainability dimensions (environment, social capital, human capital, business model and innovation, leadership and governance); Financial materiality orientation; Now incorporated by reference in IFRS S1
primary_use_case: Industry-specific sustainability disclosure for investors, primarily by US-listed companies; reference standard for materiality assessment; component of ISSB IFRS S1 implementation.
common_criticisms: Industry-specific approach can fragment cross-industry comparability; investor-only orientation rejected by stakeholder-focused critics; financial-materiality scoping narrower than double-materiality regimes (e.g., EU CSRD); transition into ISSB has created some interpretation uncertainty for issuers with established SASB-aligned reporting; sector classification quirks for companies that span industries.
primary_sources: SASB (2018). SASB Standards (codified); IFRS Foundation (2023). IFRS S1 General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information (incorporating SASB)

name: GRI
one_line_summary: Most widely used sustainability reporting framework with universal, sector, and topic standards.
extended_summary: The Global Reporting Initiative is an independent, multi-stakeholder international standard-setter for sustainability reporting, founded in 1997 by Boston-based CERES and the Tellus Institute with early backing from the UN Environment Programme. The current GRI Standards (introduced in 2016 in modular form, with the Universal Standards substantially revised in 2021) are organized into Universal Standards (foundational and management approach), Sector Standards (industry-specific topics), and Topic Standards (specific economic, environmental, and social topics). GRI's defining commitment is to a multi-stakeholder, double-materiality orientation — reporting on impacts on the economy, environment, and people regardless of whether those impacts are financially material to the reporting entity — distinguishing it from the investor-focused, financial-materiality framing of SASB and the ISSB. GRI is the most widely used sustainability reporting framework globally, particularly in Europe and emerging markets, and is referenced as a supported framework in the EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) ESRS.
originators: CERES (Coalition for Environmentally Responsible Economies); Tellus Institute; subsequently independent GRI organization based in Amsterdam
year_or_decade: 1997 (founded); 2000 (G1 first guidelines); 2016 (GRI Standards modular format); 2021 (Universal Standards revision)
core_components: Universal Standards (GRI 1: Foundation; GRI 2: General Disclosures; GRI 3: Material Topics); Sector Standards (industry-specific, ongoing rollout); Topic Standards (economic, environmental, social topics); Multi-stakeholder governance; Double-materiality orientation; Reporting principles (accuracy, balance, clarity, comparability, completeness, sustainability context, timeliness, verifiability)
primary_use_case: Comprehensive sustainability reporting on economic, environmental, and social impacts for stakeholders beyond investors; widely used reference standard in voluntary corporate sustainability reports; referenced by EU CSRD/ESRS as compatible reporting basis.
common_criticisms: Multi-stakeholder breadth criticized by investor-focused users as diluting financial-materiality signal; reporting bloat — large organizations produce hundred-page GRI reports of uneven utility; topic standards' update cadence trails emerging issues; voluntary nature limits enforcement; tension and partial overlap with ISSB IFRS S1/S2 has created reporter burden where both frameworks are used.
primary_sources: GRI (2016, revised 2021). GRI Universal Standards; GRI. Sector Standards and Topic Standards (ongoing publications)

name: LEED
aliases: Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design
one_line_summary: USGBC certification system for green buildings across categories like energy, water, materials, and indoor environment.
extended_summary: LEED is the certification system developed and administered by the US Green Building Council for environmentally sustainable design, construction, and operation of buildings and neighborhoods. The framework awards points across credit categories (Location and Transportation, Sustainable Sites, Water Efficiency, Energy and Atmosphere, Materials and Resources, Indoor Environmental Quality, Innovation, and Regional Priority), with point totals corresponding to four certification levels: Certified (40-49 points), Silver (50-59), Gold (60-79), and Platinum (80+). Distinct rating systems address different project types — Building Design and Construction, Interior Design and Construction, Building Operations and Maintenance, Neighborhood Development, Homes, and Cities and Communities — with the rating system selected and substantially adapted to project context. LEED has gone through major versions roughly every five to seven years (v1 1998, v2 2000, 2009/v3, v4 2013, v4.1 2019), with LEED v5 in development to substantially expand decarbonization and resilience requirements.
core_components: Eight credit categories (Location and Transportation, Sustainable Sites, Water Efficiency, Energy and Atmosphere, Materials and Resources, Indoor Environmental Quality, Innovation, Regional Priority); Four certification levels (Certified, Silver, Gold, Platinum); Multiple rating systems by project type (BD+C, ID+C, O+M, ND, Homes, Cities); Prerequisites and credits with point allocations; Third-party certification by Green Business Certification Inc. (GBCI)
primary_use_case: Voluntary green-building certification for design, construction, and operations; municipal incentive programs and code references; corporate real estate sustainability commitments; tenant and developer marketing differentiation.
common_criticisms: Predicted-versus-actual energy performance gaps documented in post-occupancy studies; point-based system can encourage gaming through low-impact 'points-shopping'; documentation cost is substantial particularly for smaller projects; international applicability limited by US-centric assumptions in some credits; competing standards (BREEAM, Living Building Challenge, WELL) target overlapping but distinct goals.
primary_sources: USGBC (2013). LEED v4 Reference Guides; USGBC (2019). LEED v4.1 (multiple rating system documents)
